Les Olog-hai présentent les facultés les plus développées parmi les grandes variétés guerrières de la fin du Troisième Âge, notamment lorsqu'ils doivent exécuter des manœuvres simples et agir sous les ordres de capitaines expérimentés. Ces qualités demeurent cependant distinctes d'une instruction savante. Un Troll peut connaître parfaitement les dangers de son territoire sans savoir lire, tandis qu'un autre peut comprendre les ordres d'une garnison sans posséder le vocabulaire nécessaire à une conversation prolongée avec un étranger.

Les enseignements liés à la magie demeurent exceptionnels. Les Trolls figurent principalement parmi les serviteurs employés pour leur force et leur résistance, particulièrement dans les armées des puissances de l'Ombre. Les récits ne leur attribuent aucune tradition magique commune, et leurs dispositions naturelles ne doivent pas être assimilées à la possession de pouvoirs surnaturels librement maîtrisés. Dans MERP-UI, les possibilités professionnelles demeurent étroitement encadrées, les traditions de Middle Earth for RMU réservant généralement aux Trolls les voies les plus directement associées au combat, notamment Guerrier, Roublard et Barbare. Les éventuelles adaptations liées à d'autres Professions ou à certaines variantes doivent respecter les compatibilités déjà définies dans le module, sans modification des mécaniques RMU.

Les Trolls parmi les autres peuples

Les relations des Trolls avec les autres peuples sont profondément marquées par les guerres et les attaques qui ont jalonné leur histoire. Les Elfes les connaissent comme d'anciens serviteurs de Morgoth, tandis que les Hommes les rencontrent surtout dans les régions sauvages ou parmi les armées de Sauron. Leur force et leur taille provoquent une crainte compréhensible, particulièrement lorsque des voyageurs découvrent les traces de leur passage ou les restes d'un campement attaqué. Les Khazâd possèdent une expérience particulière des Trolls des cavernes, dont la présence peut compromettre l'exploitation d'une mine ou rendre dangereux les passages souterrains. Les Hobbits, quant à eux, connaissent les Trolls de pierre à travers les récits et les dangers rencontrés dans l'Eriador, où leur discrétion et leur petite taille peuvent parfois leur permettre d'échapper à des adversaires beaucoup plus puissants.

Les Orcs entretiennent avec les Trolls des relations plus régulières, particulièrement lorsqu'ils occupent les mêmes forteresses ou participent aux armées de l'Ombre. Ils peuvent exploiter leur puissance pour accomplir des travaux, défendre un passage ou attaquer des ennemis retranchés, mais doivent également tenir compte de leur comportement et des dangers que représentent certaines variétés peu disciplinées. Les Trolls les plus puissants peuvent imposer leur volonté à des individus plus faibles, tandis que d'autres demeurent dépendants des capitaines capables de leur fournir nourriture et équipement. Ces relations ne constituent pas nécessairement une alliance fondée sur la confiance, particulièrement lorsque plusieurs groupes cherchent à contrôler les mêmes ressources. Les Olog-hai disposent d'une organisation plus étroitement liée aux ordres de Sauron, dont l'autorité détermine en grande partie leur place dans les armées de la fin du Troisième Âge.

Un Troll aventurier doit donc affronter des difficultés considérables lorsqu'il cherche à voyager parmi les Peuples Libres. Son apparence risque de provoquer immédiatement la peur et peut conduire les habitants à prendre les armes avant même qu'il ait pu expliquer ses intentions. Les portes des villes, les auberges et les passages conçus pour les Hommes ou les Nains ne sont généralement pas adaptés à sa stature, tandis que ses besoins alimentaires et ses difficultés face à la lumière peuvent compliquer l'organisation d'une expédition. Ces contraintes doivent conserver leur importance dans l'aventure, particulièrement lorsqu'un personnage tente de trouver une place parmi des compagnons qui possèdent des habitudes et des attentes très différentes des siennes. Les relations nouvelles peuvent néanmoins être développées dans le cadre d'une campagne, à condition de reposer sur des circonstances précises et sur une interprétation cohérente avec la nature du personnage.

Les Trolls à travers les Âges

Au Premier Âge, les Trolls servent principalement les entreprises de Morgoth, particulièrement dans les grandes forteresses du Nord et au sein des armées engagées contre les Elfes et les Hommes du Beleriand. Leur force est employée dans les travaux militaires, les gardes et les assauts, tandis que leur histoire demeure largement soumise aux décisions de maîtres beaucoup plus puissants qu'eux. La Guerre de la Colère entraîne ensuite la destruction des principales forces de l'Ombre et la dispersion des survivants. Au Deuxième Âge, certains Trolls vivent dans les montagnes et les régions éloignées, tandis que Sauron rassemble progressivement de nouvelles armées et emploie leur puissance au service de ses entreprises. Les communautés dont l'existence se poursuit loin des grands royaumes conservent leurs propres repaires et leurs habitudes, particulièrement lorsqu'elles disposent de territoires suffisamment isolés pour échapper aux guerres.

Au Troisième Âge, les Trolls occupent de nombreuses régions, notamment les Landes d'Etten, les Monts Brumeux, les territoires entourant la Moria et les montagnes du Mordor. Les anciennes variétés poursuivent leur existence dans les régions sauvages, tandis que Sauron emploie des Trolls dans ses armées et développe progressivement les Olog-hai, dont les qualités exceptionnelles apparaissent pendant les dernières décennies de cet Âge. Les grandes batailles de la Guerre de l'Anneau témoignent de leur puissance, particulièrement lorsque les Trolls du Mordor participent aux assauts contre les défenses des Peuples Libres. Au Quatrième Âge, la chute de Sauron provoque la dispersion et la désorganisation de ses serviteurs. Le destin précis des anciennes populations demeure peu documenté, tandis que celui des Olog-hai doit être envisagé à travers leur dépendance particulière envers la volonté de leur maître. Les campagnes peuvent explorer la survie des Trolls établis dans les régions éloignées, particulièrement lorsque les transformations du monde les conduisent à rechercher de nouvelles ressources ou à quitter leurs anciens repaires.

Incarner un Troll

Jouer un Troll en Terre du Milieu, c'est incarner un personnage dont la force et les dispositions physiques dépassent celles de la plupart des autres peuples, mais dont l'existence demeure soumise à des contraintes particulièrement importantes. Sa taille, ses besoins alimentaires, ses facultés sensorielles et sa relation avec la lumière solaire dépendent de la variété à laquelle il appartient. Son éducation et son expérience déterminent ensuite les connaissances réellement acquises, les territoires qu'il connaît et les relations qu'il entretient avec les autres habitants de la Terre du Milieu. Un personnage peut avoir grandi dans une caverne, parmi un petit groupe de Trolls des collines ou au sein d'une garnison organisée par les puissances de l'Ombre. Chacune de ces origines lui donne des habitudes et des motivations différentes, dont les conséquences doivent être prises en compte lorsqu'il quitte son environnement familier.

Un Troll des cavernes peut connaître les galeries situées sous une montagne, les mouvements d'air qui révèlent certaines ouvertures et les passages fréquentés par les animaux. Il possède une expérience des territoires souterrains dont ses compagnons peuvent tirer parti, particulièrement lorsqu'ils doivent retrouver un chemin ou reconnaître la présence d'intrus. Son départ peut résulter de l'effondrement d'une galerie, de la disparition de ses anciennes ressources ou de l'arrivée d'une population orque qui cherche à s'emparer de son territoire. Il peut également avoir été employé par un chef militaire, puis abandonné après une défaite. Les déplacements à la surface constituent cependant une difficulté majeure, particulièrement lorsque son exposition au soleil peut entraîner une pétrification définitive. Le Meneur doit donc s'assurer que le cadre de l'aventure permet réellement au personnage de participer aux déplacements et aux entreprises du groupe.

Un Troll des forêts possède une expérience différente. Il peut avoir grandi dans une région boisée, appris à reconnaître les passages empruntés par les animaux et découvert les endroits où installer un repaire protégé. Son intelligence pratique peut lui permettre d'employer des outils simples, de préparer des pièges ou de surveiller les déplacements des étrangers. Il peut quitter son territoire après une attaque, rechercher un nouveau refuge ou être attiré par les ressources d'une région dont il a entendu parler. Sa familiarité avec les bois lui sera précieuse pendant les voyages, mais les grands espaces découverts et les régions densément habitées peuvent lui présenter des dangers inhabituels. Son apparence et ses besoins alimentaires compliquent également les relations avec les populations humaines, particulièrement lorsqu'il doit obtenir de la nourriture sans recourir aux méthodes employées dans son ancien repaire.

Un Troll des collines peut appartenir à un petit groupe installé dans les Landes d'Etten ou dans les territoires rocheux des Monts Brumeux. Il connaît les cavernes, les passages et les lieux où les voyageurs font parfois halte, tandis que ses compagnons partagent avec lui les ressources de leur région. Une querelle concernant le butin, la nourriture ou la possession du repaire peut provoquer son départ, particulièrement lorsqu'il refuse de se soumettre à un individu plus puissant. Il peut également être contraint de quitter sa demeure après l'arrivée d'une force militaire ou la disparition des animaux dont il se nourrit. Sa robustesse lui permet de transporter de lourdes charges, mais ses difficultés face au soleil et son manque d'expérience des communautés étrangères exigent de véritables adaptations. Les possessions qu'il conserve peuvent également représenter une part importante de son histoire personnelle, notamment lorsqu'un objet particulier lui rappelle un ancien compagnon ou une entreprise dont il est fier.

Un Troll de pierre peut avoir vécu pendant de nombreuses années dans un repaire isolé, accumulant des objets pris aux voyageurs et apprenant à reconnaître les chemins qui lui permettent de chasser pendant la nuit. Son existence repose sur une connaissance limitée mais approfondie de son territoire, particulièrement lorsque certains passages demeurent sûrs à l'approche du jour. Une erreur peut cependant avoir des conséquences définitives, puisque l'exposition directe au soleil transforme son corps en pierre. Un tel personnage convient donc principalement à une campagne dont les déplacements et les lieux d'aventure permettent de respecter cette particularité. Son départ peut résulter de la destruction de son repaire, d'une rivalité avec d'autres Trolls ou de la recherche de nouvelles ressources, mais l'organisation de son voyage doit toujours tenir compte de son incapacité à demeurer en terrain découvert pendant la journée.

Un Troll des neiges peut appartenir aux régions les plus froides de la Terre du Milieu, où il a appris à reconnaître les passages, les proies et les abris dissimulés par la neige. Sa force et son endurance lui permettent de poursuivre de longues marches, particulièrement lorsqu'il connaît les dangers du terrain. Il peut avoir vécu seul pendant de nombreuses années, ce qui rendra difficiles ses premières relations avec des compagnons habitués à prendre des décisions collectives. Son départ peut être provoqué par la disparition du gibier, une catastrophe naturelle ou la recherche d'un territoire moins disputé. Les règles particulières concernant sa transformation sous la lumière directe du soleil doivent cependant être respectées, notamment lorsqu'il quitte les régions septentrionales pour entreprendre un voyage dans des terres plus tempérées.

Un Olog-hai possède une histoire profondément différente. Il appartient aux grandes créatures guerrières développées par Sauron à la fin du Troisième Âge et peut avoir reçu une formation au combat, à l'exécution des ordres et à l'emploi d'armes adaptées à sa stature. Il connaît le parler noir et les habitudes des garnisons dans lesquelles il a servi, particulièrement lorsqu'il a participé aux campagnes du Mordor. Sa puissance et son intelligence pratique peuvent faire de lui un combattant redoutable, mais sa dépendance envers la volonté de Sauron constitue une particularité fondamentale. Une campagne située après la chute du Seigneur des Ténèbres doit donc définir avec une grande prudence les conditions dans lesquelles un tel personnage pourrait encore exister et conserver ses facultés. Son éventuelle présence au Quatrième Âge relève d'une adaptation exceptionnelle, dont les conséquences historiques et mécaniques doivent être clairement établies avec le Meneur.

Le caractère du personnage peut varier considérablement. Certains Trolls recherchent principalement la nourriture, la sécurité et la possession d'un territoire, tandis que d'autres sont animés par la colère, la rivalité ou le désir de dominer les individus plus faibles. Un personnage peut conserver une familiarité durable avec les compagnons de son ancien repaire, éprouver de la méfiance envers les étrangers ou reconnaître l'autorité d'un chef dont il admire la puissance. D'autres peuvent être conduits à développer des relations inhabituelles, particulièrement lorsqu'un voyageur leur rend un service important ou lorsqu'ils découvrent les avantages d'une coopération qu'ils n'avaient jamais envisagée auparavant. Ces possibilités doivent demeurer cohérentes avec les capacités et l'histoire du Troll, sans transformer systématiquement les anciennes créatures de l'Ombre en individus possédant les usages et les valeurs des sociétés humaines.

Les difficultés pratiques occupent une place essentielle dans son interprétation. La taille du personnage peut lui interdire certains passages, compromettre sa dissimulation ou rendre impossible son accueil dans des bâtiments ordinaires. Ses besoins alimentaires exigent une attention particulière, notamment lorsque la compagnie traverse des territoires où les provisions demeurent limitées. La lumière solaire constitue un danger majeur pour plusieurs variétés, tandis que les réactions des autres peuples rendent difficiles les déplacements dans les régions habitées. Un Troll peut être utile pour transporter des charges, déplacer des obstacles ou défendre ses compagnons contre des adversaires puissants, mais ces qualités ne compensent pas automatiquement les contraintes que sa présence impose à une expédition. Le groupe doit donc apprendre à organiser ses déplacements en tenant compte de ses particularités, particulièrement lorsque ses compagnons appartiennent à des Races dont les besoins et les habitudes demeurent très différents.

Les possibilités professionnelles des Trolls doivent demeurer conformes aux restrictions de MERP-UI. Les traditions de Middle Earth for RMU privilégient les Professions directement liées à la force et à l'expérience pratique du combat, notamment Guerrier, Roublard et Barbare. Ces voies peuvent être envisagées selon la variété du personnage, la formation qu'il a reçue et les règles de compatibilité déjà définies. Un Troll élevé dans une forteresse peut avoir appris à manier des armes lourdes, tandis qu'un individu des forêts possède une expérience des déplacements discrets et de la chasse. La maîtrise des compétences demeure cependant distincte des caractéristiques naturelles de la Race, et les facultés extraordinaires de certains individus ne doivent pas justifier l'accès automatique à des disciplines incompatibles avec leur formation.

La Race Trolls — Tereg appartient aux Races restreintes de MERP-UI. Son utilisation peut être envisagée à travers les quatre Âges de la Terre du Milieu, selon les disponibilités et les variantes effectivement prévues par le module. Les Trolls anciens sont présents dès le Premier Âge, tandis que les Olog-hai apparaissent seulement à la fin du Troisième Âge. Les différences entre les Trolls des cavernes, des forêts, des collines, des neiges, de pierre et les Olog-hai doivent être préservées, particulièrement lorsqu'elles concernent leur stature, leurs facultés sensorielles et les effets de la lumière solaire. Les Demi-Trolls, issus des développements de MERP concernant une ascendance mêlée avec les Hommes, constituent une Race restreinte distincte et ne doivent pas être assimilés aux Olog-hai.

Avant de valider la création d'un Troll, le joueur et le Meneur devraient déterminer sa variété, son territoire d'origine, les individus auprès desquels il a grandi et les activités auxquelles il a été habitué. Ils doivent également préciser son rapport aux autres peuples, les circonstances de son départ et les moyens par lesquels il pourra prendre part aux aventures de la compagnie. Ces éléments sont particulièrement importants lorsque le personnage possède une taille exceptionnelle, une vulnérabilité solaire majeure ou une histoire étroitement liée aux puissances de l'Ombre. Son existence peut être motivée par la recherche d'un refuge, la protection d'un ancien compagnon, la volonté d'échapper à un maître ou le désir de conquérir un territoire dont il pourra disposer librement. Les événements de la campagne détermineront ensuite les relations qu'il développera et les décisions dont il acceptera la responsabilité.

Un Troll possède une force immense et une constitution dont la puissance dépasse celle de la plupart des habitants de la Terre du Milieu. Son existence demeure cependant soumise aux limites de sa nature, aux nécessités de son environnement et à l'héritage des puissances qui ont longtemps employé son peuple. Les territoires qu'il connaît, les individus auxquels il demeure attaché et les choix qu'il accomplira donneront à cette puissance une signification particulière, qu'il poursuive l'existence brutale de ses ancêtres ou cherche à trouver une place différente dans un monde qui le considère presque toujours avec crainte.

Trolls — The Tereg

In a cavern in the Ettenmoors, a Troll lifts a heavy stone that partially obstructs the entrance to his lair. Rain has washed earth into the passage, and several rocks broke loose from the hillside during the night. He sweeps the smaller stones aside with one hand, then braces his shoulder against a boulder and manages to roll it to the edge of the path. Behind him, two of his companions examine the provisions brought back from their latest expedition. One searches among the bags for a piece of meat kept for several days, while the other inspects a chest stolen from travellers. Its contents are of little use for their subsistence, but several glittering coins attract his attention. An argument breaks out when he refuses to share them. The first Troll abandons his work and returns to the cavern, furious to hear his companions quarrelling over objects whose true value none of them understands. He snatches the chest from them and sets it down in a recess already piled with broken weapons, utensils, and goods taken from travellers. Outside, the rain is beginning to cease. They will soon have to close the entrance and find somewhere to await nightfall, for the first light of day will shortly appear beyond the hills.

Beneath the Misty Mountains, in a gallery long abandoned by the Dwarves, another Troll advances with his hands against the walls. His eyes can scarcely distinguish the obstacles, but he recognises the way by the currents of air, the smells, and the particular echoes of the passages. For several days, unusual noises have reached him from a chamber beyond an ancient shaft. He stops, places one hand against the rock, and listens to the dull blows repeated at regular intervals. Inhabitants of a neighbouring gallery are working to reopen a collapsed passage. The Troll knows these sounds: he heard them before when Orcs entered the lower levels, disturbing the animals upon which he feeds. He continues towards a narrow opening, where the smell of a recently lit fire confirms the presence of intruders. The passage remains too small for him to enter, but the wall is old and some of its stones have begun to loosen. He sets about tearing one free, then another, sending fragments falling into the adjoining gallery and forcing the workers to interrupt their labour.

At the end of the Third Age, on the mountainous borders of Mordor, an Olog-hai receives his equipment before the gates of a fortress. Two Orcs check the fastenings of his cuirass while a captain shows him the position he must occupy in the company. He towers above the soldiers gathered around him, and his strength allows him to wield a hammer whose weight would quickly exhaust a Man. Unlike the ancient Trolls, he can endure sunlight and continue marching throughout the day, provided that Sauron's will continues to sustain his nature. He understands orders given in the Black Speech, recognises the signals of his troop, and can carry out the simple manoeuvres his commanders have taught him. When the company leaves the fortress, he takes his place behind the front ranks. The Orcs accompanying him keep clear of his movements, particularly when he must pass through a narrow opening. He knows that his task will be to break down gates and shatter enemy formations, but he has also learned to await the necessary command before charging. His power remains at the service of a master whose will determines much of his existence.

All belong to the Trolls, whom Elven traditions designate by the Sindarin name Torog, while MERP developments also employ the form Tereg to refer to their people. Their immense stature, formidable strength, and bodily toughness distinguish them from most inhabitants of Middle-earth. Their origins reach back to the earliest days of the Shadow, when Morgoth sought to command creatures capable of rivalling the living beings whose power he envied. Successive generations inhabited mountains, hills, forests, and caverns before Sauron gathered certain populations into his armies. Their existence is generally associated with violence, remote territories, and the enterprises of the Dark Lords, but the different varieties of Trolls possess characteristics and habits that deserve to be distinguished. Some live in small groups around a lair, others range across extensive territories in search of food, while the most formidable serve in military companies whose organisation far exceeds the capabilities of the older populations. For player characters, this diversity allows unusual lives to be envisaged, profoundly shaped by the physical demands of their nature and by the difficulties their presence creates among other peoples.

Creatures of the Earliest Days of the Shadow

The origins of Trolls remain uncertain, although their history is closely associated with the enterprises of Morgoth. In the ancient tales, Treebeard explains that Trolls were fashioned by the Dark Lord in mockery of the Ents, reproducing their immense strength without possessing their nature or wisdom. This tradition expresses an essential characteristic of Morgoth's works: unable truly to create life himself, he sought to deform existing beings and produce servants through whom he could fight the powers that opposed him. The account does not, however, definitively establish the nature of the earliest Trolls or the beings from which they might have originated. Tolkien himself continued to question their origins and the possibility that different varieties possessed distinct histories.

The first Trolls appeared in the darkness of the Elder Days, when the world had not yet known the light of the Sun. They were reputed to be massive, clumsy, and possessed of rudimentary intelligence, but their strength made them particularly useful instruments in Morgoth's armies. The great fortresses of the Shadow could employ them to carry heavy loads, maintain certain structures, or assault enemy positions, especially when obstacles had to be destroyed through sheer physical power. Trolls took part in the wars of Beleriand, where their presence is notably attested among the guards of Gothmog, Captain of the Balrogs. During the Nirnaeth Arnoediad, they fought against Húrin, whose heroic resistance and the many enemies he slew became celebrated in the tales of the Edain.

Morgoth's defeat brought about the dispersal of some of the populations that had served his armies. Certain Trolls found refuge in mountains and remote regions, while others remained associated with the powers of the Shadow that continued to exert their influence in Middle-earth. Their existence continued throughout the following Ages, but their different communities developed according to the territories they occupied and the masters to whom they were subjected. Tolkien's accounts thus describe Trolls living freely in the wilderness, others accompanying Orcs through caverns, and great creatures employed by Sauron in his military campaigns. These circumstances show that their history extends beyond that of a single, uniformly organised population, particularly when the different varieties possess noticeably distinct abilities and behaviours.

Immense Strength and Skin as Hard as Stone

Trolls tower far above Men and the Khazâd. Their bodies are massive, their chests broad, and their limbs powerful enough to move loads that a group of ordinary workers would find exceedingly difficult to lift. Their arms are often particularly long, with thick hands capable of grasping great stones, tearing certain obstacles from the ground, or wielding weapons of disproportionate size. Their gait may appear heavy, but this impression should not lead one to underestimate their ability to cross difficult terrain or move swiftly when pursuing prey. Their appearance varies between populations: some possess thick, rough skin, while others display protrusions, scaly plates, or features adapted to caverns and mountainous regions. The oldest individuals may appear almost indistinguishable from the surrounding rock, particularly when their bodies bear thick, irregular surfaces.

Their strength is their most obvious quality, but their physical resilience is of comparable importance. Trolls can endure tremendous exertion, carry heavy objects, and continue a task long after less robust beings would have been forced to stop. Their skin affords remarkable natural protection, particularly against blows and superficial injuries, although suitable weapons and experienced adversaries can inflict serious wounds upon them. Their bodily power exempts them neither from fatigue, nor from the need to feed, nor from the consequences of severe injury. Some warriors can continue fighting despite wounds that would have incapacitated a Man, but such endurance must never be confused with invulnerability. Their size may also become a disadvantage when they must pass through narrow openings, conceal themselves, or enter buildings designed for peoples of ordinary stature.

Their sensory faculties depend more closely upon their variety and environment. Trolls living in caverns may possess excellent hearing, a keen sense of smell, and particular sensitivity to vibrations, while those inhabiting hills rely more heavily upon sight and familiarity with the territories they roam. These dispositions favour certain activities, but their practical effectiveness depends upon personal experience. A Troll able to recognise the movements of an animal in a dark gallery may struggle to distinguish a traveller's tracks upon an exposed road, while an individual accustomed to mountainous regions may feel ill at ease in great forests. In MERP-UI, such differences are represented by the characteristics particular to the various Troll variants, without confusing the natural dispositions of the Race with skills acquired over the years.

Sunlight and Petrification

Sunlight constitutes one of the principal weaknesses of ancient Trolls. Stone-trolls, in particular, cannot endure direct exposure: when the rays of the Sun strike them, their bodies turn to stone and they remain permanently petrified. This phenomenon appears in the account of the three Trolls encountered by Bilbo, Thorin, and their companions, whose quarrel continues until daybreak and brings about their end. Fear of the Sun profoundly influences the existence of these creatures, especially when they must organise their movements, search for prey, or choose a lair. Caves, covered passages, and deep valleys offer valuable shelter, while a route requiring several hours across open ground may become impossible to follow at certain times of year.

The developments of MERP and Middle Earth for RMU distinguish several forms of vulnerability according to variety. Cave-trolls and Stone-trolls are particularly exposed to permanent petrification, while Hill-trolls may, under these rules, recover their normal form when exposure to sunlight ceases. Snow-trolls receive special treatment: their bodies may turn to ice under direct sunlight, then return to their former state when conditions permit. These distinctions belong to the game's adaptations and specify the consequences of sunlight for each variant, without constituting a uniform body of rules established in Tolkien's accounts. They nevertheless have considerable importance for character creation, since they determine the hours during which a character may travel and the dangers he must face.

Fear of exposure to sunlight also influences relationships between Trolls. A group must know the locations of shelters, estimate the time required for a journey, and recognise passages that remain protected during the day. A prolonged quarrel or a hunt begun too late may lead to a situation whose consequences are irreversible. Experienced individuals therefore learn to recognise seasonal changes, landforms that remain in shadow, and signs announcing sunrise. This caution is not universal, since certain varieties better tolerate diffuse light, while the Olog-hai possess exceptional dispositions enabling them to act in full daylight under Sauron's dominion. The exact nature of these advantages and weaknesses must remain consistent with the characteristics already defined in MERP-UI.

Cave-trolls

Cave-trolls inhabit the depths of mountains, ancient mines, and underground passages seldom frequented by other peoples. Their existence is particularly adapted to darkness and enclosed spaces, where they can find shelter during periods when the lands outside are exposed to the Sun. Tolkien's accounts notably mention a Cave-troll accompanying the Orcs who attacked the members of the Fellowship of the Ring in Moria. Its scaly skin, massive foot, and physical power bear witness to the dangers posed by such a creature when it attempts to force a passage. Great doors and obstacles designed to slow adversaries of ordinary stature may give way beneath its blows, particularly when it possesses sufficient space to employ its full strength.

In the developments of Middle Earth for RMU, these Trolls possess extremely poor eyesight, compensated for by particularly acute hearing, smell, and touch. They learn to recognise the echoes of galleries, the movement of air, and the smells left by animals or intruders. This adaptation enables them to move through passages unknown to other inhabitants, particularly where darkness makes torches indispensable to travellers. Their existence nevertheless remains dependent upon available resources: they seek prey, occupy sufficiently spacious areas, and may come into conflict with underground populations when they attempt to expand their territory. Certain Orcs learn to lure or employ them during attacks, but directing creatures so powerful and poorly disciplined carries considerable dangers, even for those familiar with their habits.

A character belonging to this variety may possess extensive experience of galleries, ancient shafts, and underground passages, particularly when he has lived for many years within a particular region. He may know how to recognise the movements of neighbouring populations, places where water can be found, and openings leading to other areas. His knowledge nevertheless remains closely bound to his environment. The surface, great open spaces, and journeys beneath the light of the Sun present major difficulties, whose consequences must be considered before introducing him into an adventuring company.

Forest-trolls

Forest-trolls are a variant developed within MERP traditions. They live in small groups within wooded regions, particularly where trees, ravines, and uneven terrain provide sufficiently spacious shelter. Their appearance remains massive and threatening, but they are described as less crudely clumsy than certain other varieties, with cunning and attentiveness to the terrain that may surprise travellers. They know how to employ simple tools, particularly knives, slings, and traps, and may learn to recognise paths regularly used by animals. Forests also provide them with wood, stones, water, and numerous opportunities for concealment, especially where the undergrowth remains thick.

Their existence depends upon thorough knowledge of the areas they inhabit. A Troll may know the locations of hollow trees, sheltered caverns, or ravines whose walls provide protection against bad weather. He may know where game regularly passes, recognise certain smells, and watch the paths taken by travellers. Groups established in a particular region must nevertheless possess sufficient resources to feed several individuals whose needs are considerable. A forest heavily frequented by other inhabitants or depleted by hunting may force them to move their lair, especially when neighbouring populations attempt to deny them access to certain resources. These constraints give their movements a territorial logic and allow characters to be envisaged whose practical knowledge rests upon many years of experience.

Sunlight remains dangerous to these Trolls, even when foliage diminishes its effects. The rules adapted in Middle Earth for RMU specify their limited ability to act in diffuse light and the consequences of direct exposure. A character must therefore know where he can find shelter and avoid journeys that might expose him to the Sun without protection. Hunting, tracking, and trap-setting skills result from personal experience, particularly when he has learned to recognise the movements of animals and the habits of strangers travelling through his territory.

Hill-trolls and Stone-trolls

Hill-trolls live chiefly in rugged regions, rocky moorlands, and territories where numerous caverns allow them to establish lairs. The Ettenmoors, north of Rivendell, are among the lands traditionally associated with their presence, while Sauron's armies also employ great Trolls from Gorgoroth. These creatures possess remarkable strength and can wield exceedingly heavy weapons, particularly clubs, hammers, or great stones used as projectiles. Individuals living in small groups search their territories for resources and sometimes accumulate goods taken from travellers, especially when certain objects attract their attention without necessarily possessing any immediate usefulness.

Stone-trolls are among the most familiar representatives of their people. The three creatures encountered by Bilbo and the Dwarves in the lands of Eriador possess a lair where they have accumulated objects, provisions, and riches stolen from travellers. They speak a crude form of the Common Speech, readily quarrel, and may be distracted from their intentions by an argument. Their behaviour shows that they can recognise certain goods, maintain a fire, and make simple decisions, even if their imprudence and limited ability to foresee distant consequences render them particularly vulnerable to the tricks of an experienced adversary. Their petrification at sunrise constitutes one of the most famous images in their history, recalling that strength alone cannot overcome the limits imposed upon their nature.

The distinctions between Hill-trolls and Stone-trolls may be further defined according to gaming traditions. Middle Earth for RMU notably distinguishes their stature, certain physical peculiarities, and the consequences of exposure to sunlight. These varieties nevertheless possess comparable habits when living in small groups, particularly in their manner of seeking provisions, defending a lair, and dividing accumulated possessions. For a character, knowledge of hills, rocky passages, and shelters suitable for remaining hidden during the day may become essential, while conflicts with companions sometimes explain his departure or his desire to seek a territory he can occupy alone.

Snow-trolls

Snow-trolls occupy a particular place among the creatures of the Far North. Tolkien mentions them notably through a comparison concerning Helm Hammerhand, whose strength and exploits in the snow recall the power attributed to these beings. The accounts do not, however, provide any detailed description of their communities or habits. MERP developments allow Trolls adapted to frozen regions to be envisaged, living in the northern mountains, snow-covered valleys, and territories where other populations remain scarce. Their existence then rests upon the search for food, knowledge of passages, and the ability to pursue prey under particularly demanding conditions.

These creatures are described as solitary or living in very small groups. Their size and endurance enable them to cover long distances, particularly when pursuing an animal or traveller whose tracks they have discovered. Cold regions offer them shelter in caverns, rocky hollows, and certain passages protected from the wind. Human communities of the North may preserve stories concerning their presence, particularly where expeditions have disappeared or herds have been attacked in remote regions. The developments of Middle Earth for RMU assign them a remarkable peculiarity: under direct sunlight, their bodies turn to ice before gradually recovering their original nature when exposure ceases. This transformation belongs to the rules specific to the variant, whose consequences must be respected in MERP-UI.

A Snow-troll character may possess thorough knowledge of frozen landscapes, passages concealed by snowdrifts, and the dangers threatening travellers unfamiliar with these regions. He may nevertheless quickly discover the limits of his experience upon leaving the Far North, particularly if he must cross wooded territories, human cities, or temperate regions whose resources he does not know. His appearance and stature also make relations difficult with populations that regard Trolls as dangerous predators. Such an origin is therefore chiefly suited to campaigns whose geographical setting and possibilities for travel can accommodate its particular characteristics.

The Olog-hai, Sauron's Black Trolls

The Olog-hai represent a new form of Troll that appeared towards the end of the Third Age. Their existence is directly associated with the enterprises of Sauron, who sought to command warriors combining the strength of the ancient creatures with superior faculties of discipline and coordination. They appear notably in the southern regions of Mirkwood, as well as upon the mountainous borders of Mordor, where their presence contributes to strengthening the armies of the Dark Lord. Tolkien describes them as powerful, agile, and cunning creatures whose skin remains particularly resistant. They tower above even the greatest Orcs, and their strength enables them to wield equipment intended for warriors of exceptional stature.

Their ability to endure sunlight constitutes one of their most important characteristics. Unlike the older varieties, the Olog-hai can act during the day for as long as Sauron's will continues to exert its power over them. This dependence binds them profoundly to the Dark Lord, whose disappearance brings about the collapse of the authority sustaining part of their faculties. They know the Black Speech of Barad-dûr and can understand the orders required for their military employment. Their behaviour remains brutal and ferocious, but their intelligence allows them to participate in coordinated operations, particularly when they must defend a position, attack a fortification, or fight among disciplined troops.

The Olog-hai thus occupy a particular place in the armies of the late Third Age. Their physical power makes them suited to assaults, while their robustness enables them to carry weapons and protection adapted to their size. Some fight with great hammers, shields, or metal equipment whose manufacture requires specialised workshops. They may be charged with breaking down gates, shattering an enemy formation, or defending a particularly important passage. Their effectiveness nevertheless remains dependent upon their training, the organisation of their troops, and the commands they receive. In MERP-UI, the Olog-hai must be distinguished from common Trolls, particularly because of their special abilities and late appearance. Their presence during the First or Second Age would be inconsistent with the established chronology.

Lairs, Groups, and Daily Life

Trolls possess no uniform society comparable to the kingdoms of Men or the great Houses of the Khazâd. Their settlements depend chiefly upon their variety, available resources, and the authority to which they are subjected. Some live alone in caverns or difficult-to-reach regions, while others occupy small lairs shared with several companions. Larger concentrations are chiefly found among creatures employed by the powers of the Shadow, when captains must gather enough Trolls for labour and military campaigns. Their daily existence is dominated by material needs: finding food, possessing shelter suited to their size, and avoiding dangers threatening their survival. Strength often allows them to seize coveted resources, but keeping them also requires knowledge of the territory and the habits of its other inhabitants.

Their dietary needs represent an important constraint. A Troll must obtain considerable quantities of food, particularly when he regularly undertakes demanding physical exertion. Groups living in wild regions may hunt animals, seek carcasses, or attack herds and travellers. Some carry recovered provisions back to their lairs, while others consume their catches immediately and must soon set out again in search of new resources. Trolls associated with an army depend more heavily upon supplies organised by their masters, especially when military movements take them through territories where hunting alone would be insufficient. A captain may therefore employ several workers to prepare the loads and stores required by a company of great creatures, whose upkeep represents a considerable expense.

Possession of objects may also play an important role in their habits. Trolls in wild regions sometimes accumulate goods recovered during expeditions, particularly when glittering or unusual objects attract their attention. They may keep weapons, chests, vessels, and articles whose true purpose they do not understand, while others chiefly seek food and equipment necessary for their activities. Such possessions sometimes become the subject of quarrels, especially when several individuals believe they contributed to acquiring them. A sufficiently powerful chief may impose a division of the goods or simply seize those he covets, while a less organised group risks losing considerable time in disputes that compromise the safety of its members.

Families and the Transmission of Habits

Tolkien's accounts reveal almost nothing about Troll reproduction, childhood, or the forms of kinship they might maintain. The different varieties must nevertheless possess means of perpetuating their populations, particularly when their presence continues across several Ages. MERP developments leave the Gamemaster the possibility of defining family groups, close relationships, or settlements where young Trolls gradually learn the behaviours necessary for survival. These possibilities remain interpretations intended for the game, however, and no particular family organisation should be presented as an institution universally established by Tolkien.

A young Troll raised in a cavern may learn to recognise the passages of his territory, the smells of animals, and the dangers associated with sunlight. He gradually discovers where food can be found and the boundaries of regions frequented by other creatures. An individual belonging to a hill group may watch the adults, learn to move stones that close a lair, or recognise travellers carrying goods of interest. Young Trolls growing up under the authority of a power of the Shadow may receive much more restrictive instruction, particularly when their masters intend to prepare them for labour or military functions. Such apprenticeships determine much of their knowledge, while the physical characteristics of their variety provide the natural dispositions upon which they can build.

Personal relationships remain difficult to generalise. Some Trolls may maintain lasting familiarity with companions who share their lair, while others are chiefly concerned with defending their resources. An individual may recognise the authority of a stronger chief, remain attached to a territory he has occupied for a long time, or display a measure of loyalty towards those who have fed and protected him. The Olog-hai, whose existence is directly connected with Sauron's enterprises, experience particular conditions of training and command. Such differences allow characters possessing personal histories to be conceived without attributing identical institutions, traditions, or feelings to every variety.

Tools, Weapons, and Heavy Labour

The strength of Trolls favours the use of exceptionally large tools and weapons. Individuals living in wild regions may employ rocks, heavy sticks, clubs, or objects recovered among goods taken from travellers. Some develop particular skill in wielding these weapons, especially when they have learned to fight adversaries capable of avoiding their blows. Creatures employed by Sauron sometimes possess equipment manufactured specifically for their stature, including hammers, shields, and metal protection. Using such equipment requires genuine experience, for a powerful but clumsy fighter may prove vulnerable against trained opponents who know how to exploit the slowness of certain movements or the constraints imposed by the terrain.

Trolls can also perform work beyond the physical capabilities of other peoples. The armies of Morgoth and Sauron employ them to carry heavy loads, move materials, and destroy obstacles. During the siege of Minas Tirith, great Mountain-trolls notably help carry the battering ram Grond, whose enormous weight would have been impossible to move swiftly without tremendous strength. Cave-trolls may tear stones from a wall, while Hill-trolls move boulders to close or defend a passage. These abilities nevertheless depend upon circumstances, for their strength does not replace the knowledge required to construct a stable structure or manufacture a complex mechanism.

Craft skills therefore differ greatly between individuals. A Troll may know how to repair a club, move stones within a lair, or prepare shelter without possessing the knowledge of a genuine builder. Another, raised among Orcish craftsmen or long employed in the works of a fortress, may acquire more extensive experience of tools and techniques necessary for certain activities. Mastery of a trade depends upon upbringing and the skills actually developed, without physical strength automatically granting knowledge of materials. This distinction constitutes an important aspect of character creation, especially when a Troll's activities extend beyond those of a warrior or a creature chiefly concerned with finding food.

Languages and Understanding the World

Trolls possess varying linguistic abilities. The earliest populations described in Tolkien's traditions had an extremely rudimentary language, but contact with Orcs and the influence of Sauron gradually contributed to the development of their means of communication. The Stone-trolls of Eriador notably speak a crude form of the Common Speech, while the Olog-hai know the Black Speech employed in the armies of Barad-dûr. These differences reflect the history of their communities and the instruction received, particularly where certain creatures remain isolated from other peoples for long periods. Trolls of the wilderness may possess a vocabulary limited to ordinary activities, while those serving in garrisons learn the orders and expressions needed for the tasks entrusted to them.

Their intelligence must be considered according to variety and experience. Some Trolls are clumsy, quarrelsome, and easily deceived, particularly when they cannot foresee the consequences of an unfamiliar situation. Others possess genuine cunning, recognise travellers' habits, or understand the advantages of an ambush. The Olog-hai display the most developed faculties among the great warrior varieties of the late Third Age, particularly when required to execute simple manoeuvres and act under the orders of experienced captains. These qualities nevertheless remain distinct from scholarly instruction. A Troll may know the dangers of his territory perfectly well without being able to read, while another may understand the commands of a garrison without possessing the vocabulary needed for a prolonged conversation with a stranger.

Instruction in the magical arts remains exceptional. Trolls appear chiefly among servants employed for their strength and resilience, particularly in the armies of the powers of the Shadow. The accounts attribute no common magical tradition to them, and their natural dispositions must not be equated with freely mastered supernatural powers. In MERP-UI, professional possibilities remain closely restricted, with the traditions of Middle Earth for RMU generally reserving for Trolls the paths most directly associated with combat, particularly Fighter, Rogue, and Barbarian. Any adaptations involving other Professions or particular variants must respect the compatibilities already defined by the module, without changing RMU mechanics.

Trolls Among the Other Peoples

The relationships of Trolls with other peoples are profoundly marked by the wars and attacks that have characterised their history. The Elves know them as ancient servants of Morgoth, while Men chiefly encounter them in wild regions or among Sauron's armies. Their strength and size inspire understandable fear, particularly when travellers discover the traces of their passage or the remains of an attacked camp. The Khazâd possess particular experience of Cave-trolls, whose presence may compromise the exploitation of a mine or make underground passages dangerous. Hobbits, meanwhile, know Stone-trolls through tales and dangers encountered in Eriador, where their discretion and small stature may sometimes allow them to escape opponents far more powerful than themselves.

Orcs maintain more regular relations with Trolls, particularly when they occupy the same fortresses or participate in the armies of the Shadow. They may exploit their power to carry out work, defend a passage, or attack entrenched enemies, but must also take account of their behaviour and the dangers posed by certain poorly disciplined varieties. The most powerful Trolls may impose their will upon weaker individuals, while others remain dependent upon captains capable of providing food and equipment. Such relationships do not necessarily constitute an alliance founded upon trust, particularly when several groups seek control of the same resources. The Olog-hai possess an organisation more closely bound to Sauron's orders, whose authority largely determines their place in the armies of the late Third Age.

A Troll adventurer must therefore confront considerable difficulties when attempting to travel among the Free Peoples. His appearance is likely to provoke immediate fear and may lead inhabitants to take up arms before he has even been able to explain his intentions. City gates, inns, and passages designed for Men or Dwarves are generally unsuited to his stature, while his dietary needs and difficulties with sunlight may complicate the organisation of an expedition. These constraints must retain their importance during the adventure, particularly when a character attempts to find a place among companions whose habits and expectations differ greatly from his own. New relationships may nevertheless develop within a campaign, provided they rest upon specific circumstances and an interpretation consistent with the character's nature.

Trolls Through the Ages

During the First Age, Trolls chiefly serve the enterprises of Morgoth, particularly within the great northern fortresses and the armies engaged against the Elves and Men of Beleriand. Their strength is employed in military labour, guard duties, and assaults, while their history remains largely subject to the decisions of masters far more powerful than themselves. The War of Wrath subsequently brings about the destruction of the principal forces of the Shadow and the dispersal of the survivors. During the Second Age, certain Trolls inhabit mountains and remote regions, while Sauron gradually gathers new armies and employs their strength in his enterprises. Communities living far from the great kingdoms preserve their own lairs and habits, especially when they possess territories sufficiently isolated to escape the wars.

During the Third Age, Trolls inhabit numerous regions, notably the Ettenmoors, the Misty Mountains, the territories surrounding Moria, and the mountains of Mordor. The older varieties continue their existence in wild regions, while Sauron employs Trolls in his armies and gradually develops the Olog-hai, whose exceptional qualities appear during the final decades of this Age. The great battles of the War of the Ring bear witness to their power, particularly when the Trolls of Mordor participate in assaults against the defences of the Free Peoples. During the Fourth Age, Sauron's downfall brings about the dispersal and disorganisation of his servants. The precise fate of the older populations remains poorly documented, while that of the Olog-hai must be considered in light of their particular dependence upon their master's will. Campaigns may explore the survival of Trolls established in remote regions, particularly when transformations of the world lead them to seek new resources or abandon their former lairs.

Playing a Troll

Playing a Troll in Middle-earth means portraying a character whose strength and physical dispositions exceed those of most other peoples, but whose existence remains subject to particularly important constraints. His size, dietary needs, sensory faculties, and relationship with sunlight depend upon the variety to which he belongs. His upbringing and experience then determine the knowledge he has actually acquired, the territories he knows, and the relationships he maintains with the other inhabitants of Middle-earth. A character may have grown up in a cavern, among a small group of Hill-trolls, or within a garrison organised by the powers of the Shadow. Each of these origins gives him different habits and motivations, whose consequences must be taken into account when he leaves his familiar surroundings.

A Cave-troll may know the galleries beneath a mountain, the currents of air that reveal certain openings, and the passages frequented by animals. He possesses experience of underground territories from which his companions may benefit, particularly when they must rediscover a route or recognise the presence of intruders. His departure may result from the collapse of a gallery, the disappearance of his former resources, or the arrival of an Orcish population seeking to seize his territory. He may also have been employed by a military chief, then abandoned after a defeat. Travel upon the surface nevertheless presents a major difficulty, particularly when exposure to sunlight may cause permanent petrification. The Gamemaster must therefore ensure that the setting of the adventure genuinely allows the character to participate in the group's journeys and undertakings.

A Forest-troll possesses different experience. He may have grown up in a wooded region, learned to recognise the paths followed by animals, and discovered places where a sheltered lair could be established. His practical intelligence may enable him to employ simple tools, prepare traps, or watch the movements of strangers. He may leave his territory after an attack, seek a new refuge, or be attracted by the resources of a region about which he has heard. His familiarity with the woods will prove valuable during journeys, but great open spaces and densely inhabited regions may present unfamiliar dangers. His appearance and dietary needs also complicate relationships with human populations, particularly when he must obtain food without resorting to the methods employed in his former lair.

A Hill-troll may belong to a small group settled in the Ettenmoors or the rocky territories of the Misty Mountains. He knows the caverns, passages, and places where travellers sometimes halt, while his companions share the resources of their region with him. A quarrel concerning plunder, food, or possession of the lair may provoke his departure, particularly when he refuses to submit to a stronger individual. He may also be forced to abandon his dwelling after the arrival of a military force or the disappearance of the animals upon which he feeds. His robustness enables him to carry heavy loads, but his difficulties with sunlight and lack of experience of foreign communities demand genuine adaptations. The possessions he keeps may also represent an important part of his personal history, particularly when a certain object reminds him of a former companion or an undertaking of which he remains proud.

A Stone-troll may have lived for many years in an isolated lair, accumulating objects taken from travellers and learning to recognise the paths that allow him to hunt during the night. His existence rests upon a limited but thorough knowledge of his territory, particularly where certain passages remain safe as daybreak approaches. A mistake may nevertheless have permanent consequences, since exposure to direct sunlight turns his body to stone. Such a character is therefore chiefly suited to a campaign whose journeys and locations allow this peculiarity to be respected. His departure may result from the destruction of his lair, rivalry with other Trolls, or the search for new resources, but the organisation of his travels must always account for his inability to remain in exposed terrain during the day.

A Snow-troll may come from the coldest regions of Middle-earth, where he has learned to recognise paths, prey, and shelters concealed by snow. His strength and endurance enable him to undertake long marches, particularly when he understands the dangers of the terrain. He may have lived alone for many years, making his first relationships with companions accustomed to collective decisions difficult. His departure may be provoked by the disappearance of game, a natural disaster, or the search for a territory less fiercely contested. The particular rules concerning his transformation under direct sunlight must nevertheless be respected, especially when he leaves the northern regions to travel through more temperate lands.

An Olog-hai possesses a profoundly different history. He belongs to the great warrior creatures developed by Sauron towards the end of the Third Age and may have received training in combat, the execution of orders, and the use of weapons suited to his stature. He knows the Black Speech and the habits of the garrisons in which he served, particularly if he took part in the campaigns of Mordor. His strength and practical intelligence may make him a formidable warrior, but his dependence upon Sauron's will constitutes a fundamental peculiarity. A campaign set after the downfall of the Dark Lord must therefore establish with great caution the conditions under which such a character might still exist and retain his faculties. His possible presence in the Fourth Age constitutes an exceptional adaptation, whose historical and mechanical consequences must be clearly established with the Gamemaster.

The character's temperament may vary considerably. Some Trolls chiefly seek food, security, and possession of a territory, while others are driven by anger, rivalry, or the desire to dominate weaker individuals. A character may maintain lasting familiarity with the companions of his former lair, feel mistrust towards strangers, or recognise the authority of a chief whose power he admires. Others may be led to develop unusual relationships, particularly when a traveller renders them an important service or they discover the advantages of cooperation they had never previously considered. These possibilities must remain consistent with the Troll's abilities and history, without systematically transforming the ancient creatures of the Shadow into individuals possessing the customs and values of human societies.

Practical difficulties occupy an essential place in his portrayal. The character's size may prevent him from using certain passages, compromise his concealment, or make it impossible for him to be accommodated in ordinary buildings. His dietary needs demand particular attention, especially when the company crosses territories where provisions remain limited. Sunlight constitutes a major danger for several varieties, while the reactions of other peoples make travel through inhabited regions difficult. A Troll may prove useful for carrying loads, moving obstacles, or defending his companions against powerful adversaries, but these qualities do not automatically compensate for the constraints his presence imposes upon an expedition. The group must therefore learn to organise its journeys with his particular characteristics in mind, especially when his companions belong to Races whose needs and habits are very different from his own.

The professional possibilities of Trolls must remain consistent with the restrictions of MERP-UI. The traditions of Middle Earth for RMU favour Professions directly connected with strength and practical combat experience, particularly Fighter, Rogue, and Barbarian. These paths may be considered according to the character's variety, the training he has received, and the compatibility rules already established. A Troll raised in a fortress may have learned to wield heavy weapons, while an individual from the forests possesses experience of stealthy movement and hunting. Mastery of skills nevertheless remains distinct from the natural characteristics of the Race, and the extraordinary faculties of certain individuals must not justify automatic access to disciplines incompatible with their training.

The Trolls — Tereg Race belongs to the Restricted Races of MERP-UI. Its use may be considered throughout the four Ages of Middle-earth, according to the availability and variants actually provided by the module. Ancient Trolls are present from the First Age onwards, while the Olog-hai appear only towards the end of the Third Age. The differences between Cave-trolls, Forest-trolls, Hill-trolls, Snow-trolls, Stone-trolls, and Olog-hai must be preserved, especially where they concern stature, sensory faculties, and the effects of sunlight. Half-trolls, originating in MERP developments concerning mixed ancestry with Men, constitute a distinct Restricted Race and must not be confused with the Olog-hai.

Before approving the creation of a Troll, the player and Gamemaster should determine his variety, territory of origin, the individuals among whom he grew up, and the activities to which he became accustomed. They should also establish his relationship with other peoples, the circumstances of his departure, and the means by which he may take part in the company's adventures. These considerations are particularly important when the character possesses exceptional size, a major vulnerability to sunlight, or a history closely associated with the powers of the Shadow. His existence may be motivated by the search for refuge, the protection of a former companion, the desire to escape a master, or the ambition to claim a territory he can control freely. The events of the campaign will then determine the relationships he develops and the decisions for which he accepts responsibility.

A Troll possesses immense strength and a constitution whose power exceeds that of most inhabitants of Middle-earth. His existence nevertheless remains subject to the limits of his nature, the necessities of his environment, and the legacy of the powers that have long employed his people. The territories he knows, the individuals to whom he remains attached, and the choices he makes will give that strength a particular meaning, whether he continues the brutal existence of his ancestors or seeks to find a different place in a world that almost always regards him with fear.

system.description:
Trolls — Les Tereg

Dans une caverne des Landes d'Etten, un Troll soulève une lourde pierre qui obstrue partiellement l'entrée de son repaire. La pluie a entraîné de la terre dans le passage, et plusieurs rochers se sont détachés de la pente pendant la nuit. Il dégage les plus petits d'un revers de main, puis cale son épaule contre un bloc qu'il parvient à faire rouler jusqu'au bord du chemin. Derrière lui, deux de ses compagnons examinent les provisions rapportées au cours de leur dernière expédition. L'un cherche parmi les sacs une pièce de viande conservée depuis plusieurs jours, tandis que l'autre inspecte une caisse dérobée à des voyageurs. Les objets qu'elle contient ne présentent guère d'intérêt pour leur subsistance, mais plusieurs pièces brillantes attirent son attention. Une querelle éclate lorsqu'il refuse de les partager. Le premier Troll abandonne son travail et retourne dans la caverne, furieux d'entendre ses compagnons se disputer pour des objets dont aucun ne connaît véritablement la valeur. Il leur arrache la caisse et la dépose dans un renfoncement où s'entassent déjà des armes brisées, des ustensiles et des marchandises prises aux voyageurs. Dehors, la pluie commence à cesser. Il faudra bientôt fermer l'entrée et trouver un endroit où attendre la nuit, car les premières lueurs du jour apparaîtront derrière les collines.

Sous les Monts Brumeux, dans une galerie abandonnée depuis longtemps par les Nains, un autre Troll avance en s'aidant de ses mains contre les parois. Ses yeux distinguent à peine les obstacles, mais il reconnaît le chemin grâce aux courants d'air, aux odeurs et aux résonances particulières des passages. Depuis plusieurs jours, des bruits inhabituels lui parviennent d'une salle située au-delà d'un ancien puits. Il s'arrête, pose une main contre la roche et écoute les coups sourds qui se répètent à intervalles réguliers. Des habitants d'une galerie voisine travaillent à rouvrir un passage effondré. Le Troll connaît ces bruits : il les a déjà entendus lorsque des Orcs ont pénétré dans les niveaux inférieurs, dérangeant les animaux dont il se nourrit. Il poursuit sa marche jusqu'à une ouverture étroite, où l'odeur d'un foyer récent lui confirme la présence d'intrus. Le passage demeure trop petit pour lui permettre de s'y introduire, mais la paroi est ancienne et certaines pierres ont commencé à se détacher. Il entreprend d'en arracher une, puis une seconde, faisant tomber dans la galerie voisine des fragments qui obligent les travailleurs à interrompre leurs travaux.

À la fin du Troisième Âge, aux frontières montagneuses du Mordor, un Olog-hai reçoit son équipement devant les portes d'une forteresse. Deux Orcs vérifient les attaches de sa cuirasse pendant qu'un capitaine lui montre la place qu'il devra occuper dans la compagnie. Sa taille dépasse largement celle des soldats rassemblés autour de lui, et sa force lui permet de manier un marteau dont le poids épuiserait rapidement un Homme. Contrairement aux anciens Trolls, il peut supporter la lumière du soleil et poursuivre sa marche pendant la journée, pourvu que la volonté de Sauron continue de soutenir sa nature. Il connaît les ordres du parler noir, reconnaît les signaux de sa troupe et comprend les manœuvres simples que ses chefs lui ont enseignées. Lorsque la compagnie quitte la forteresse, il prend place derrière les premiers rangs. Les Orcs qui l'accompagnent se tiennent à distance de ses mouvements, particulièrement lorsqu'il doit franchir un passage étroit. Il sait que sa tâche sera d'enfoncer les portes et de rompre les formations ennemies, mais il a également appris à attendre le commandement nécessaire avant de s'élancer. Sa puissance demeure au service d'un maître dont la volonté détermine une grande partie de son existence.

Tous appartiennent aux Trolls, que les traditions elfiques désignent par le nom sindarin Torog, tandis que les développements de MERP emploient également la forme Tereg pour évoquer leur peuple. Leur stature immense, leur force redoutable et la dureté de leur corps les distinguent de la plupart des habitants de la Terre du Milieu. Leurs origines remontent aux premiers temps de l'Ombre, lorsque Morgoth cherchait à disposer de créatures capables de rivaliser avec les êtres vivants dont il enviait la puissance. Les générations successives occupèrent les montagnes, les collines, les forêts et les cavernes, avant que Sauron ne réunisse certaines de leurs populations dans ses armées. Leur existence demeure généralement associée à la violence, aux territoires reculés et aux entreprises des Seigneurs des Ténèbres, mais les différentes variétés de Trolls présentent des caractères et des habitudes qui méritent d'être distingués. Certains vivent en petits groupes autour d'un repaire, d'autres parcourent des régions étendues à la recherche de nourriture, tandis que les plus redoutables servent dans des compagnies militaires dont l'organisation dépasse largement les capacités des anciennes populations. Pour les personnages joueurs, cette diversité permet d'envisager des existences singulières, profondément marquées par les exigences physiques de leur nature et par les difficultés qu'entraîne leur présence parmi les autres peuples.

Les créatures des premiers temps de l'Ombre

Les origines des Trolls demeurent incertaines, bien que leur histoire soit étroitement associée aux entreprises de Morgoth. Dans les récits anciens, Sylvebarbe explique que les Trolls furent façonnés par le Seigneur des Ténèbres en dérision des Ents, dont ils reproduiraient la force immense sans posséder leur nature ni leur sagesse. Cette tradition exprime une caractéristique essentielle de l'œuvre de Morgoth : incapable de créer véritablement la vie par lui-même, il cherchait à déformer les êtres existants et à produire des serviteurs qui lui permettraient de combattre les puissances auxquelles il s'opposait. Le récit ne permet cependant pas de déterminer de manière définitive la nature des premiers Trolls, ni les êtres dont ils auraient pu être issus. Tolkien lui-même conserva des interrogations concernant leur origine et la possibilité que différentes variétés possèdent des histoires distinctes.

Les premiers Trolls apparurent dans les ténèbres des Jours Anciens, alors que le monde ne connaissait pas encore la lumière du Soleil. Ils étaient réputés massifs, maladroits et dotés d'une intelligence rudimentaire, mais leur force faisait d'eux des instruments particulièrement utiles aux armées de Morgoth. Les grandes forteresses de l'Ombre pouvaient les employer au transport des charges, à l'entretien de certains ouvrages ou à l'assaut des positions ennemies, particulièrement lorsque des obstacles devaient être détruits par la seule puissance physique. Les Trolls participèrent aux guerres du Beleriand, où leur présence est notamment attestée parmi les gardes de Gothmog, capitaine des Balrogs. Lors de la Nirnaeth Arnoediad, ils furent opposés à Húrin, dont la résistance héroïque et les nombreux ennemis abattus demeurèrent célèbres dans les récits des Edain.

La défaite de Morgoth entraîna la dispersion d'une partie des populations qui avaient servi ses armées. Certains Trolls trouvèrent refuge dans les montagnes et les régions reculées, tandis que d'autres demeurèrent associés aux puissances de l'Ombre qui continuèrent d'exercer leur influence en Terre du Milieu. Leur existence se poursuivit pendant les Âges suivants, mais leurs différentes communautés évoluèrent selon les territoires occupés et les maîtres auxquels elles furent soumises. Les récits de Tolkien décrivent ainsi des Trolls vivant librement dans les régions sauvages, d'autres accompagnant les Orcs dans les cavernes, et de grandes créatures employées par Sauron dans ses campagnes militaires. Ces situations montrent que leur histoire dépasse celle d'une population unique et uniformément organisée, particulièrement lorsque les différentes variétés possèdent des aptitudes et des comportements sensiblement distincts.

Une force immense et une peau dure comme la pierre

La stature des Trolls dépasse largement celle des Hommes et des Khazâd. Leur corps est massif, leur poitrine large et leurs membres suffisamment puissants pour déplacer des charges qu'un groupe de travailleurs ordinaires aurait beaucoup de difficulté à soulever. Les bras sont souvent particulièrement longs, avec des mains épaisses capables de saisir de grandes pierres, de déraciner certains obstacles ou de manier des armes disproportionnées. Leur démarche peut paraître lourde, mais cette impression ne doit pas conduire à sous-estimer leur capacité à franchir des terrains difficiles ou à avancer rapidement lorsqu'ils poursuivent une proie. Leur apparence varie selon les populations : certains possèdent une peau épaisse et rugueuse, tandis que d'autres présentent des excroissances, des plaques écailleuses ou des caractères adaptés aux cavernes et aux régions montagneuses. Les individus les plus anciens peuvent paraître presque indissociables de la roche qui les entoure, particulièrement lorsque leur corps présente des surfaces épaisses et irrégulières.

Leur force constitue leur qualité la plus évidente, mais leur résistance physique possède une importance comparable. Les Trolls peuvent supporter des efforts considérables, transporter des objets lourds et poursuivre une tâche longtemps après que des êtres moins robustes auraient dû interrompre leur travail. Leur peau offre une protection naturelle remarquable, particulièrement contre les coups et les blessures superficielles, même si des armes appropriées et des adversaires expérimentés peuvent leur infliger des blessures graves. La puissance de leur corps ne les soustrait ni à la fatigue, ni à la nécessité de se nourrir, ni aux conséquences de dommages importants. Certains combattants sont capables de continuer à se battre malgré des blessures qui auraient neutralisé un Homme, mais cette endurance ne doit jamais être confondue avec une invulnérabilité. Leur taille peut également devenir une difficulté lorsqu'ils doivent franchir des passages étroits, se dissimuler ou pénétrer dans des constructions prévues pour les peuples de stature ordinaire.

Leurs facultés sensorielles dépendent davantage de leur variété et de leur environnement. Les Trolls vivant dans les cavernes peuvent posséder une excellente ouïe, un odorat développé et une sensibilité particulière aux vibrations, tandis que ceux des collines s'appuient davantage sur leur vue et sur la connaissance des territoires qu'ils parcourent. Ces dispositions favorisent certaines activités, mais leur efficacité réelle dépend de l'expérience personnelle. Un Troll capable de reconnaître les mouvements d'un animal dans une galerie obscure peut éprouver des difficultés à distinguer les traces d'un voyageur sur une route découverte, tandis qu'un individu habitué aux régions montagneuses peut se montrer peu à l'aise dans les grandes forêts. Dans MERP-UI, ces différences sont représentées par les caractéristiques propres aux différentes variantes de Trolls, sans confondre les dispositions naturelles de la Race avec les compétences acquises au cours des années.

Le soleil et la pétrification

La lumière solaire constitue l'une des principales faiblesses des Trolls anciens. Les Trolls de pierre, notamment, ne peuvent supporter son exposition directe : lorsqu'ils se trouvent atteints par les rayons du soleil, leur corps se transforme en pierre et ils demeurent définitivement pétrifiés. Ce phénomène apparaît dans le récit des trois Trolls rencontrés par Bilbon, Thorin et leurs compagnons, dont la querelle prolongée jusqu'au lever du jour provoque leur disparition. La peur du soleil influence profondément l'existence de ces créatures, particulièrement lorsqu'elles doivent organiser leurs déplacements, rechercher des proies ou choisir un repaire. Les grottes, les passages couverts et les vallées encaissées constituent des refuges précieux, tandis qu'un itinéraire dont le franchissement exige plusieurs heures en terrain découvert peut devenir impossible à certaines périodes de l'année.

Les développements de MERP et de Middle Earth for RMU distinguent plusieurs formes de vulnérabilité selon les variétés. Les Trolls des cavernes et les Trolls de pierre sont particulièrement exposés à une pétrification définitive, tandis que les Trolls des collines peuvent, selon ces règles, retrouver leur apparence lorsque cesse l'exposition au soleil. Les Trolls des neiges reçoivent un traitement particulier : leur corps peut se transformer en glace sous les rayons directs, puis retrouver son état initial lorsque les conditions le permettent. Ces différences appartiennent aux adaptations du jeu et précisent les conséquences de la lumière pour chacune des variantes, sans constituer un ensemble de règles uniformément établi dans les récits de Tolkien. Elles possèdent cependant une portée considérable pour la création d'un personnage, puisqu'elles déterminent les heures auxquelles il pourra voyager et les dangers auxquels il devra faire face.

La peur de l'exposition solaire influence également les relations entre Trolls. Un groupe doit savoir où se trouvent les refuges, évaluer le temps nécessaire à un déplacement et reconnaître les passages qui demeurent protégés pendant la journée. Une querelle prolongée ou une chasse entreprise trop tard peuvent conduire à une situation dont les conséquences seront irréversibles. Les individus les plus expérimentés apprennent donc à connaître les variations des saisons, les reliefs qui conservent l'ombre et les signes annonçant le lever du soleil. Cette prudence n'est pas universelle, puisque certaines variétés supportent mieux la lumière diffuse, tandis que les Olog-hai possèdent des dispositions exceptionnelles leur permettant d'agir en plein jour sous la domination de Sauron. La nature exacte de ces avantages et de ces faiblesses doit demeurer conforme aux caractéristiques déjà définies dans MERP-UI.

Les Trolls des cavernes

Les Trolls des cavernes occupent les profondeurs des montagnes, les anciennes mines et les passages souterrains rarement fréquentés par les autres peuples.
